analysis.one_liner: Restricts health-status discrimination, caps preexisting-condition exclusions, and makes continued employer coverage cheaper.
analysis.headline: Introduced in May 1995 with 10 Republican cosponsors, the bill never left the House Ways and Means Committee and died without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred health plans and insurers from setting eligibility, enrollment, or premium rules based on a person's health history, and would have capped preexisting-condition exclusions at six months (with credit for prior coverage). It also would have required guaranteed renewal of policies and made it cheaper for laid-off or divorced family members to keep employer coverage. Plans and insurers that violated the rules would owe an excise tax equal to 25 percent of their premiums.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers changing or losing jobs who have health problems, people whose new plans would otherwise impose preexisting-condition exclusions, and spouses or children dropped from coverage around a divorce. Families adopting children and women with pregnancies would get explicit protection.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Sick workers changing or losing jobs

how_it_helps.text: Bars group health plans and insurers from imposing eligibility, enrollment, or contribution requirements based on health status, medical history, claims experience, or disability.

Limits preexisting-condition exclusions to conditions diagnosed or treated in the prior 3 months and exclusion periods to 6 months (12 for late enrollees), with credit for prior coverage and exceptions for pregnancy, newborns, and adopted children.
Requires insurers to renew coverage except for nonpayment, fraud, or a uniformly applied discontinuation of a whole class of coverage.

Requires plans to offer lower-cost COBRA continuation alternatives at 69% or 52% of the standard premium, and closes a loophole so spouses or children dropped from coverage in the 12 months before a divorce can still elect continuation coverage.
Enforces the standards with a tax equal to 25% of a noncompliant plan's annual premiums (or self-insured plan's expenditures), with waivers for good-faith, quickly corrected failures.
Keeps end-stage renal disease patients eligible for Medicare from losing their COBRA continuation coverage.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers that sponsor self-insured plans, which would face the 25% excise tax for noncompliance, lose the ability to screen out sick applicants, and take on cheaper-coverage mandates. Some compliance costs could be passed into premiums.

drawbacks.text: Plans could satisfy the cheaper-coverage requirement by offering COBRA alternatives worth only half or two-thirds of the richest plan, so a displaced worker choosing the low-premium option could end up with significantly skimpier benefits.

The bill does not ban preexisting-condition exclusions outright — it still permits a 6-month exclusion window (12 months for late enrollees) — and it does not regulate how premiums are set for individual coverage, so insurers could still price people with expensive conditions out of the market.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people with health problems, the portability and nondiscrimination rules were the difference between continuous coverage and a gap that could follow them for years; the costs fell on insurers and plan sponsors through compliance and the excise tax. The bill's main design weakness is that its affordability fix for COBRA comes by letting people buy thinner coverage, and its refusal to touch premium-setting leaves a hole for the individual market. On balance a modest, targeted consumer-protection bill rather than a broad overhaul.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and its Health Subcommittee in May 1995 and sat there until the Congress ended, never getting a markup or a floor vote — though Congress enacted very similar portability and preexisting-condition protections the following year in HIPAA.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 10, 1995 by Rep. Nancy Johnson of Connecticut and referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
On May 18, 1995 it was referred to the Health Subcommittee, and no further action was ever taken on it for the rest of the 104th Congress.
The bill's original cosponsors were 10 House Republicans, and no version of the bill ever reached the House floor for a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers that sponsor health plans avoided the 25% excise tax exposure and the new underwriting restrictions. Workers with preexisting conditions kept bearing coverage gaps for another year, until Congress passed substantially similar portability rules in HIPAA in 1996.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers, until HIPAA passed

sides.party_line_note: All 11 sponsors and cosponsors were House Republicans, but the bill drew no recorded floor vote or committee action, so no opposition votes exist to measure the split.

industries.note: The bill would bar them from using health status to screen or price applicants, cap preexisting-condition exclusions, and force guaranteed renewal, backed by a 25% excise tax on premiums for noncompliance. Their business model of avoiding sick customers is exactly what the bill targets, so industry interest ran against the bill's beneficiaries.

Plan sponsors would owe a tax equal to 25% of health coverage expenditures if their plans violated the standards, and would have to offer cheaper COBRA alternatives and follow the nondiscrimination rules.
